Nel giugno del 1645 i turchi mettono piede nell’isola, veneziana dal 1211 e conquistano il forte di S. Teodoro. Il suo comandante Biagio Giuliani si sacrifica con tutta la famiglia …

“Al primo assalire che fecero i Turchi di quel forte, per lo sterminato lor numero, non potè resistere il Giuliani; per cui osservando egli irrompere da tutte parti l’abborrito nemico, pensò sottrarsi, con atto magnanimo, alla servitù miserabile che lo attendeva; dare uno splendido esempio da imitare a’ suoi compagni in quella guerra; e quindi rapidamente scendendo nella conserva della polvere di sua mano vi diede fuoco, facendo saltare in aria sè, la propria moglie, i figliuoli suoi, la fortezza e gli assalitori ad un tempo, sacrando per cotal guisa sull’ altar della patria primo il suo sangue a testimoniar la sua fede … “.

Dopo vent’anni d’assedio, per la città di Candia nel 1668 è giunta l’ora decisiva. Anche i turchi sono stanchi e chiedono ai veneziani la resa, che viene sdegnosamente rifiutata dal capitano Francesco Morosini.

“In sì fatto bollore dell’ armi disperando Acmet Vìsir di superare la città con la forza, col mezzo di Nicasio Panagiotti, suo dragomano, scrisse al capitan generale Francesco Morosini, esortandolo a ceder la piazza, con promessa di farlo principe di Valachia e di Moldavia. Ma il Morosini gli rispose di questo modo: Nulla cosa è il danaro e la ricchezza. Se il re tuo signore vuole quelle cose utili e giuste ad entrambi, son pronto a condiscendere ai di lui desiderii; se sono contrarie, non ha egli tanto oro od argento per indurmi … ”

ImageDescription.value:
Zoomable full resolution image available at davidrumsey.com.

This image 3697.066 is a part of image group 3697.000.

Color copper lithograph map. Shows capitals, roads, important towns, mountains and rivers. Includes explanations. Prime meridian is Greenwich. Relief shown by hachures.

1848 edition, known as Mitchell's new Universal atlas, without Tanner's name on the title page. Tanner issued this atlas first in 1836 with engraved maps, then it was taken over by Carey and Hart in 1843 and converted by them to lithographic maps in 1845. In 1846 Mitchell took over the publishing of this atlas and continued until 1849. This atlas is important in American printing history in that it was the first American atlas to be converted from engraved map plates to lithographic map plates. The maps are in full color, lithographic, covering the World, North America, and Mexico. Oregon and Upper California maps show the new boundary of Mexico and the United States resulting from the Mexican War, for the first time. Title page by K. Knight, includes a view of "The first landing of Columbus in the new world". Print showing Christopher Columbus and crew praying after landing in the New World for the first time on October 12 1492. Atlas is bound in half leather green marbled paper covered boards with "Mitchell's Universal Atlas" stamped in gilt on front label. Mitchell was born in 1792 in Connecticut and spent some of his early working years as a teacher. During his teaching years, he became quite dissatisfied with the available textbooks, and this led him to become a writer and publisher. He moved to Philadelphia, a major center for publishing at the time.

P6106.

Mitchell, Samuel Augustus
Tanner, Henry S.

ImageDescription.value:
Zoomable full resolution image available at davidrumsey.com.

This image 4578.063 is a part of image group 4578.000.

Lithographed. Relief shown with hachures. Inset of Candia (Crete).

This is a unique copy of the Mitchell/Tanner Universal Atlas. Frederick Bourquin and his employer, Peter Duval, received a Third Premium Award from the Franklin Institute in November, 1848, for their achievement in transferring the Universal Atlas from copper plates to lithographic stones. The catalog of the exhibition lists it as "No. 52. Universal Atlas in folio, a most beautiful specimen of the art of transferring and lithographic printing, from the press of P.S. Duval, Philadelphia, transferred by Bourquin." This copy of the atlas was their submission to the Franklin Institute to be considered for the award. It is made up of sheets from the atlas, all uncolored, all oversized, and all taken from various editions of the atlas from 1846 to 1848 (one map is dated 1849, but we believe it was issued in late 1848). It appears that these sheets were offprints that remained in the lithographer's shop and that the atlas was made up from them. Atlas is bound in half leather marbled paper covered boards with leather label on the front reading "Atlas Transferred From Copper To And Printed From Stone By Frederick Bourquin." The atlas stayed with the Franklin Institute, each page having the Institute's stamp on it, and was eventually sold by the Institute in the mid twentieth century. There are several erasures of dates that are earlier than 1848 (perhaps an attempt to make the book seem up to date) and several erasures of Tanner's name (on the title page) to conform to the fact that in 1848 this was known as Mitchell's atlas. The map borders vary between the "Mitchell" and the "Tanner" borders. And the paper thickness and quality varies as well. These sheets may have been some of the first "pulls" of each map in the various 1846-48 editions. This is a fascinating compilation and throws light on the transition in printing from copper plate to lithographic stone.

Ristow p. 311 (award actually received in 1848).

Artist.value: Ottoman War Ministry Press

ImageDescription.value:
Zoomable full resolution image available at davidrumsey.com.

This image 10874.000 is a part of image group 10874.000.

Dated 1307 [1891].

"An extremely rare and highly unusual work that is probably the first accurate military map of Crete; it was made when control of the island was hotly contested between the Ottomans and its Greek majority population; printed for the use of the Ottoman high command, it was published by the War Ministry Press in Istanbul, employing extraordinary colour lithographic techniques indicative of the new German influence instilled by the great military reformer ‘Goltz Pasha’. Crete, the large island strategically guarding the approaches to the Eastern Mediterranean, and home to fabled ancient civilizations, came under Ottoman rule in 1669. While a large percentage of the indigenous Greek population converted to Islam and embraced Turkish rule, the majority of Cretans retained the Orthodox Christian faith and increasingly came to resent the Sublime Porte’s regime. Beginning in 1770, the Greek Cretans mounted a series of armed rebellions against the Ottomans, only to see their dreams repeatedly crushed by the sultan’s vastly superior forces. The rise of the Kingdom of Greece in the 1820s, in the Peloponnese, which gained its independence upon successfully rebelling against the Ottomans, encouraged the Greek Cretans to redouble their efforts towards gaining their self-determination. While the growing restlessness of the island’s Christian community, combined with international pressure from the major European powers, compelled the Ottomans to make significant political concessions to the Greek Cretans, they succeeded in reestablishing their heavy-handed rule over the island. The present map was published in 1891, just as the Ottomans were consolidating their final attempt to impose direct autocratic rule over Crete. In 1878, the island began to enjoy a wide degree of political autonomy, but in 1889 the Ottoman governor revoked these privileges, renewing a regime of oppressive rule which sparked rebellion of Greek Cretans, as well as fomenting sectarian violence between the island’s Christian and Muslim communities. The map would have been made for the exclusive use of senior Ottoman administrators and military commanders as they marshalled resources and troops to reimpose their authority over the island. They were not aware that their efforts represented the beginning of the final act of the Ottomans’ 229 year-long presence on Crete, for an alliance of the great European great powers, in league with Greek interests, would expel the Ottomans from Crete forever, in 1898. The large format map (executed to scale of 1:292,000) embraces the entire island of Crete, and accurately showcases all the features necessarily to guide strategic military planning. The island’s extreme topography, with mountains rising up beyond 8,000 feet above sea level, is expressed through carefully lithographed shading. Crete is show divided into its various districts, which are bordered by both lithographed and hand-coloured lines in bright hues, while the district names are lithographed in bright yellow characters. Predicated upon scientific military surveys, the map labels the locations of every village, including the many remote mountains hamlets where rebel activity persisted, as well as outlining the fortified walls of the major coastal cities. All roads of note are delineated, while the map carefully labels the locations of forts, windmills and rural Christian monasteries (especially important details, as these strongly built, and often fortified, edifices were habitually used as key bases by the Greek insurgents fighting Ottoman rule). The German Connection to Ottoman Military Cartography: A Worthy Topic for Further Research The present work is perhaps the first accurate printed military map of Crete, predicated upon innumerable scientific surveys and reconnaissance missions conducted by the Ottoman Army in recent years. The map is remarkable in many ways, due to its unusual design and the printing techniques employed; in these respects, it bears the hallmarks of the rising German influence upon the Ottoman military and it cartographic operations. By the early 1880s, Sultan Abdul Hamid II had become disenchanted with his traditional Western allies, Britain and France. These powers had failed to protect his empire from what he saw as Russian aggression and the insubordinate behavior of its Slavic and Greek vassals. He also balked at the severe Anglo-French interference in the Ottoman economy brought about by the Sublime Porte’s high levels of foreign debt. Germany promised to step into the void, pledging great financial, technical and military assistance, without the ‘imperialist’ strings attached. In 1883, Germany dispatched the military modernizer General Wilhelm Leopold Colmar Freiherr von der Goltz (1843 – 1916) to Istanbul to reform the Ottoman Army; he remained there until 1895. He introduced Prussian discipline and battle tactics, the most modern German equipment, as well as giving the sultan sound strategic advice as to how deal with his enemies both foreign and domestic. This had enormous effects upon the Ottoman military, giving rise the ‘Goltz Generation’ of Ottoman officers that would distinguish themselves in future military campaigns. A near hero figure in the Ottoman lands, he known by his honorific title as ‘Goltz Pasha’. He would return to the Sublime Porte’s service for his final act during World War I, where he led the sultan’s armies to great success in Iraq. Goltz, who had a keen understanding of the importance of modern scientific surveying and cartography to military success, played a key role in radically transforming the Ottoman Army’s engineering corps and its map drafting and printed operations at the Erkan-ı Harbiye-i Umumiye Matbaası (Ottoman War Ministry Press). Goltz was known to had brought German military engineers and printing technicians to Istanbul to instruct the Ottomans on how to create and reproduce scientific military surveys of the highest calibre for strategic and operational use. Up this point, the Ottoman military had some advanced cartographic capabilities, largely influenced by French techniques and styles, but these skills was unevenly applied. In some cases, the Ottoman engineers made stellar maps, done to the best European specifications, in other cases the mapping was desultory, consisting of crude sketches done to the whims of untrained amateurs. The present map was carefully compiled from a composite of scientific surveys, integrated into an accurate, picture, by Ottoman cartographers at the Erkan-ı Harbiye-i Umumiye Matbaası, but likely to the specifications, if not under the direct supervision of German mapmakers. Indeed, the map’s overall style is in line with the crisp and clear signature form of the great cartographic masters of Eastern Germany, such as Heinrich Kiepert and of the Gotha school. The map’s printing quality is very usual for Ottoman cartography of the time, in that is executed by complex overlaid layers of colour lithography, with the topographic shading over a beige background, district boundaries in printed bright colours, and regional names printed in yellow characters, while the seas appear in bold blue and with the margins in sharply contrasting bold beige. Additionally, the district borders are hand coloured in bright hues of watercolour. This technically demanding and visually arresting manner of printing is reminiscent of the style of colour lithography practiced in Leipzig. The Erkan-ı Harbiye-i Umumiye Matbaası produced further maps following the style and techniques employed upon in this work, although they tended to be more subdued. As such, the present map appears to be a fascinating transitional work, in which these styles were ‘experimented’ upon by Ottomans under German guidance. While the German role in the making of the present map is obvious, the precise nature of Goltz’s reforms upon Ottoman military cartography is not known and deserves to be a subject of further academic research. The present map is extremely rare; we have not been able to trace any other examples in institutional collections, nor are we aware of any sales records. This is not surprising, as the map would have been issued in only a very small print run for the exclusive use of senior Ottoman officials and officers; it was never for public distribution. Moreover, its large size and practical purpose, as an active strategic aid, ensured a low survival rate. Crete was home to many great ancient civilizations, and being a large, fertile island, strategically guarding the approaches to the Eastern Mediterranean, it was always fought over by the Mediterranean’s great powers. It was famously the centre of the Minoan Civilization (c.3000 – c.1100 BC), as well as a domain of various ancient Greek and Roman regimes, before coming under Byzantine rule. Crete was first ruled by Muslims, when subjects of the Abbasid Caliphate conquered the island in the 820s AD, forming the Emirate of Crete. The island subsequently retuned to Byzantine administration, from 961 to 1205, until the island came under Venetian rule. While the Cretan economy and local Greek culture flourished under the Serene Republic, the Venetians were highly oppressive and unpopular. Perhaps to the surprise of people today, many Greek Orthodox Cretans were relieved when the Ottomans conquered Crete in 1669, following the lengthy Cretan War (1645-69). While they may not have been thrilled about being ruled by a Muslim power, the Sublime Porte had traditionally shown a high degree of tolerance towards Greek Christians in their existing realm (the Greek Orthodox Church was the largest single landowner in the Ottoman Empire!). Initially, Ottoman rule on Crete was quite mild, as they left the Greek Orthodox Church to control their own affairs, while the local merchants prospered from the new trade routes that had opened up to the east. That being said, Greek Cretans were still second-class citizens on their own island, and this increasingly caused resentment. In the first decades of Ottoman rule, large portions of the indigenous Greek Orthodox population converted Islam, and it is estimated that by the mid 18th century as much as 50% of Cretans were Muslim. This mirrors the pattern in some other parts of the Ottoman Empire, such as Bosnia, where indigenous Slavs converted to Islam, but stands in contrast to the situation in other areas, such as Bulgaria, where most of the Muslim population consisted of colonists who had migrated from Anatolia. Thus, it must be noted that the Turkish Cretans were part of the true fabric of the island, and in no way ‘foreign’. In the early years, the Muslim Cretans developed their own distinct customs and culture, and while tensions developed in some places, in many cases they got along well with their Christian neighbours (it helped that Greek remained the mother tongue of all Cretans). During the first century of Ottoman rule on Crete there was no serious question of challenging the regime, as the sultan’s army and navy were so powerful that they could instantly crush any insurrection. Yet the desire of many in the Greek Cretan population to gain their self-determination never died, and a powerful underground independence movement developed. By the 1760s, the overall military strength of the Ottoman Empire was in decline. Its awesomely powerful, but large, cumbersome armies were no longer able to cope with the rapidly mobile field artillery detachments employed by their European opponents, while Western navies had developed infinitely better capabilities predicated upon new vessel design and improved tactics. Russia had a strong connection to Greece, seeing it as its true cultural antecedent. Led by Catherine the Great, Russia throttled the Ottomans during the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774. It was during this time that the Greek underground in Crete saw its first opportunity to mount a credible challenge against the Sultan’s rule. During Easter 1770, Greeks in some areas rebelled, in the expectation that a Russian fleet would arrive to back them up. While the rebels managed to temporarily gain control over parts of the island, the Russian forces never arrived, and the Ottomans crushed the insurrection. The severity of the Sublime Porte’s response alienated Greek Cretan moderates from the Sublime Porte; from that point onwards, relations between Crete’s Muslim and Christian communities were increasingly acrimonious. The Greek Cretans came to view their Muslim neighbors as ‘foreigners’, even though they shared the same ancient ancestry. From the Ottoman perspective, about half of the island was Muslim (and thus partial to the Sultan’s rule), while Crete occupied a key role in the imperial economic establishment. Far from being a far-flung colony, it was a highly valued, integral part of the empire. This was underlined by the fact that many Muslim Cretans held key roles at the Sublime Porte, creating a permanent high-level lobbying group in favour of Istanbul dedicating serious resources to preserving their rule over the island. Despite the inter-ethnic tensions, the main Cretan cities, such of Heraklion, Chania and Rethymno were extremely vibrant and prosperous trading ports, where Muslims, Christians and Jews all enjoyed a relatively high degree of freedom. The Greek War of Independence (1821-29) marked a watershed moment for Crete and the greater Ottoman Empire. Greece’s attainment of independence during the conflict (albeit controlling only on a rump of territory barely extending beyond the Peloponnese) served as an oracle to all Greek peoples - their eventual liberation from Ottoman rule was a matter of destiny! For the Ottomans, it was devastating blow, severely damaging their authority, which had been predicated upon their air of ‘invincibility’. However, despite the hopes of many Greek Cretans, there was no realistic possibility that their island would join Greece at this stage; the Ottomans made it clear that they would fight to retain Crete, while the pro-Greek European powers (Britain, France and Russia) were unwilling to act to liberate the island. Yet the independence of Greece and the dream of Enosis (‘union’ with Greece) encouraged the Cretan Greeks to continuously push for more rights, leading on a path towards their full self-determination. After a spell of Egyptian rule over Crete (the Egyptians were technically vassals of the Sublime Porte, but for a time challenged its authority, taking over large parts of the empire), the Greek Cretans rebelled in 1841, causing the sultan to grant concessions, granting the Greek community many privileges. Another uprising in 1858, compelled the sultan to award Greek Cretans full citizenship rights on the same level as Muslims. Meanwhile, the Muslim Cretans felt increasingly threatened by the Greek resurgence, and many left the island for other parts of the Ottoman Empire, fearing that Crete’s union with Greece was simply a matter of time. Cretan Muslims declined from accounting for 47% of the population in 1821 to 22% in 1858. The Greek community staged a massive uprising, known as the Great Cretan Revolt (1866-9), and while the insurgents captured large parts of the island, the Ottoman forces progressively moved in to restore control. Notably, the Ottomans massacred over 700 Greek civilians who were sheltered with the rebels at the Arkadia Monastery, which had the effect of turning global opinion sharply against the Ottomans. While the Sublime Porte vanquished the rebellion, they had to henceforth contend with constant foreign interference in their Cretan affairs. During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-8, the Ottomans were throttled. This gave the international community the leverage to compel the Sublime Porte to grant Crete limited autonomy within the Ottoman Empire, and a comprehensive power-sharing deal for the Greek Cretans (including the appointment of the island’s first Christian Governor-General). These principles were enshrined in the Halepa Charter (October 27, 1878), signed under the supervision of a British envoy. The Halepa Charter cooled tensions for a time. However, in 1889, Crete’s Muslim governor, Shakir Pasha, used the excuse of a local factional disagreement to instate martial law throughout the island, abrogating the privileges of the Greek community. This sparked a sharp two year-long rebellion against Ottoman rule, that saw horrific intercommunal violence. The present map was made for the use of the Ottoman high command in 1891, just as the sultan’s men were gaining the upper hand over the Greek insurgency yet faced the certain prospect of even great resistance in the near future. At the beginning of 1897, the Greek Cretans, once again, rebelled, but this time were supported by the great European powers, who finally had enough of what they regarded as the Sublime Porte’s unjust oppression of that the considered to be a ‘Christian’ island. In February 1897, a multinational force made up of troops from Great Britain, France, Italy, Russia, Germany and Austro-Hungary landed on Crete to restore order and to enforce a new political settlement (Germany and Austria-Hungary soon withdrew from the coalition). The occupying powers compelled Sultan Abdul Hamid II to (very reluctantly) agree to grant Crete its full internal autonomy within the Ottoman Empire on terms that exceeded that of the Halepa Charter. However, in what became known as the Candia Massacre (September 6, 1898), a group of irregular Muslim troops, in the service of the sultan, turned against the Greek community in Heraklion, killing between 500 and 800 Greek Cretans, as well as 14 British soldiers. This caused the occupying powers to order the complete expulsion of the Ottoman presence on Crete, bringing an end to the 229-year-old regime. While Crete was to technically remain a de jure part of the Ottoman Empire, Ottoman officials or troops were not allowed to even step foot on the island, which was declared the ‘Cretan State’, a fully autonomous land dominated by its Greek community. Prince George of Greece was appointed as the island’s High Commissioner (essentially governor), who ruled as an autocrat, resisting Crete’s union with Greece. Tensions broke out between factions under Prince George, on one hand, and Eleftherios Venizelos (the future Greek prime minister), who advocated Enosis (by 1906 the latter side gained the upper hand). Meanwhile, Muslim Cretans continued to leave the island, as while that were not formally expelled, they felt increasingly unwelcome in what was the only home they or their ancestors had ever known. In 1908, the pro-Enosis forces won out, as turmoil in Istanbul caused by the Young Turk Rebellion, allowed the Cretan leadership to formally sever all ties with the Ottoman Empire and to declare their island a part of the Kingdom of Greece. However, international recognition of Enosis had to wait until 1913, in the wake of the First Balkan War (1912-3), when an alliance of Greece and the Slavic Balkan powers throttled the Ottoman Army. Since that time, Crete has remained an important and integral component of the modern Greek state, with many Cretans attaining roles of great prominence in Athens (notably including Eleftherios Venizelos, who served as Greek prime minister on several occasions between 1910 and 1933). The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) that sought to resolve all outstanding issues in the wake of the World War I and the Greco-Turkish War (1919-22), enacted the cruel Greco-Turkish Population Exchange (1923), whereby all ethnic Turks and Muslims had to leave Greece, while all ethnic Greeks had to leave Turkey. Thus, the remaining Cretan Muslims, who then accounted for 7% of the island’s population, were forced to suddenly leave their homeland. Most of these refugees settled in Turkey, where many of their ancestors have retained their distinct cultural identity. Even today, it is not unusual to meet Turks living in Istanbul who describe themselves as ‘Cretans’, even though they have never set foot upon the island." (Alexander Johnson, 2021)
